newsitem.title: UK: Minor metals underpinned by light consumer demand.
newsitem.headline: Minor metals underpinned by light consumer demand.

text.p: Light consumer demand helped to underpin and lift many of the industrial minor metals over the past week, though the volume of business was not enough to punch prices significantly higher, European traders said.
Antimony firmed on a lack of Chinese offers and low stocks, while chrome, molybdendum, gallium and titanium also registered gains.
"There is demand seeping into the market, though so far there has been no major rush from the consumers to cover," one trader commented.
Opinons on the next direction of the antimony market remained divided.
Several traders suggested the recent rally from a mid-December low of $2,050/$2,150 a tonne was set to continue near-term and pegged an upside target at around $2,500 or higher.

They argued Chinese producers were holding back for higher prices and that stocks were running at low levels -- a condition that was unlikely to satisfy first and second quarter 1997 consumer requirements.
Others said the market was fast becoming overbought and was due for a downside correction following the steady gains during the early part of this year.
"I think we have seen the top for now," one trader said, while another commented, "It looks well overcooked, these are not realistic prices for the antimony market at the moment."
They said there was little in the way of consumer demand to justify such high numbers and they believed some producers may take advantage of the higherr numbers.
Both high and low nitro content chrome flew higher on the wings of demand from the aerospace industry.

Traders said most of the minor metals linked to the aerospace industry were currently experiencing upside interest. Traders said chrome shined on talk that two of the three Chinese producers are not currently producing metal, while the third had no available nearby material.

Two sources said Russian producers were late in delivering material to a market already gripped by supply tightness. Molybdenum was also underpinned by the aircraft sector and to a lesser extent from the hi-tech electronics industry. Japanese enquiry helped to lift gallium, against the backdrop of low stocks.
Demand for communication satellites and hi-tech blue laser production may spark a further rise in gallium prices.
It is used in solar panals, an energy source of many satellites, traders said.
Titanium sponge also firmed on demand from the aerospace industry.
Cobalt remained steady, while germanium bucked the trend and showed signs of heading lower.
Traders germanium's sharply higher prices over the past year had seen manufacturers of catalysts, who use germanium, switch to other metals.

"There are cheaper alternatives which give near enough the same result as germanium," one trader said. Bismuth was unmoved, but several traders expected a move higher in the second and third quarters of 1997.
